No sweat, I thought to myself. Friday afternoon, Chol Hamoed Sukkos, Kingston Avenue station, MetroCard in hand, an easy swipe-swipe, and we were both on the other side of the turnstile. Perhaps I miscalculated, because the 3-train downstairs sounded like it was about to pull out of the station. Hearts racing, we carefully made our way down the stairs as fast as humanly possible.

Unfortunately, we got to the door just as the train bell bing- bonged. The doors shut right in front of our faces—nearly pinching my nose.

“Alright,” Yossi said. “Hashgacha protis. We’ll catch the next—” Just then, the train conductor called out to us from further down the platform and motioned to us to go ahead. The doors slid open, and we yelled, “Thank you very much, sir!” above the rushing noise of the train heading in the opposite direction. He replied

long underground subway tunnel, we would reach our destination– Manhattan–where we had some serious sparks of kedusha to

we were above ground again. As an 11 year-old, I can honestly say that there’s nothing quite like the thrill of walking up the stairs of the subway leading to the street, taking in the view of massive sky-scrapers all around, and then heading off towards the first store on your mivtzoim route.

The beautiful sun and crisp Tishrei air were an added bonus. Over the last year, we’d sure seen our share of crummy mivtzoim weather. Not that bad weather ever mattered to us before. You see, this route is our responsibility. It has been since my older brother left to yeshivah in France last year. The seven store owners we visit depend on us to get their portion of Yiddishkeit for the week, and we’ve never let them down. In short, cats and dogs could be falling from the sky, but if it’s Friday, we’re on mivtzoim.

After giving neshek to a Jewish police woman, handing out Tishrei guides, and shaking lulov and esrog with about twenty different people, we quickly made our way to our first store. Rafi, an Israeli businessman, as he referred to himself, owned a successful electronics store on 6th Avenue. If not for us, he said, he wouldn’t have any Yiddishkeit in his life at all.

With a big smile, and lulov and esrog at the ready, we opened the door. Today, however, we were greeted not by Rafi, but by an unfamiliar man wearing a suit and tie. He walked towards us before we could make our way to the counter. Reading off of a small stack of papers, he called us by name.

“Yes,” I answered for both of us. The normally busy store was almost completely empty. I could sense something wasn’t right.

“Hang on, Yossi,” I whispered. Yossi was always jumping to conclusions.

Before I could finish, he said, “Rafi Adler?” I nodded my head.

“I’m afraid I have some terrible news. Sit down.” He gestured to a table that Rafi always had prepared for us with ice-cold bottles of soda. Today, the table was empty. “I am Mr. Adler’s former attorney. I’m sorry to tell you, but Mr. Adler passed away last Shabbos.”

The initial shock couldn’t leave me. Rafi, the man we’ve visited every week over the past year, the man old enough to be our zeidy, the same man who smiled each time we walked through the door, and the same man whose eyes lit up when we told him a new story of the Rebbe–gone!

“Boruch Dayan Ho’emes,” I whispered. I don’t know where I found strength to ask this next question. “Is anyone saying kaddish? I know he doesn’t have any Jewish children.”

“That’s correct.” The lawyer then jumped straight to the point. “Before his passing, Mr. Adler drafted a will in my office. Nobody but you knows

Yossi’s jaw still remained dropped this whole time.

“Mr. Adler notified me that you and your friend visit him weekly, and requested in his will that I be here to greet you the Friday after his passing. He asked you boys to arrange for someone to say kaddish for him.” The room was spinning.

“There’s one more thing here for you, Sruli,” the lawyer continued. “Mr. Adler left two envelopes for you. One contains a letter explaining everything, and the other contains a check for $500,000–Mr. Adler’s entire life savings.”

The lawyer gave me both envelopes and his business card, and asked that I call him first thing next week to set up a meeting with my parents.

I checked my watch and realized it was getting late. The words ‘Erev Shabbos’ hit my thoughts like a ton of bricks. We parted with the lawyer and ran back to the subway.

The train ride back to Kingston Avenue was a blur. The walk home—the same. Only when I noticed the large crowd of people standing outside my home did I come to my senses. What was going on? I then saw that they were reporters, all of them holding

microphones and speaking into large video cameras on the shoulders of cameramen. I walked a bit slower now, trying to take in what I saw.

Suddenly, a voice in the crowd yelled, “There he is!”

I looked behind me, but no one else was there. Could they be talking about me? Instantly, the massive group of reporters and camera-men charged towards me. Within seconds, I was completely surrounded from all sides. What on earth was going on here? The reporters pushed microphones into my face; their questions flying from every direction possible. They were all so loud; I could barely make out what anyone was saying. Then I heard something—a familiar name. As I opened my mouth, the group of reporters instantly silenced. I looked at the one who said the name.
